newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai finance firms rush to meet merger deadline.
newsitem.headline: Thai finance firms rush to meet merger deadline.

text.p: Sixteen ailing Thai finance and securities firms closed last month and given until July 11 to announce merger plans or face being taken over have been scrambling to cut last-minute deals, executives said.

With ailing firms only required to show a vague interest from a potential buyer, around half of those affected were expected to announce that a foreign party had expressed interest, they told Reuters.

The firms were among the hardest hit in a sector struggling to cope with declining revenues, high funding costs and a deterioration in asset quality as Thailand goes through its worst economic downturn in over a decade.
A high degree of interest in the closed firms on offer had been expressed by potential foreign buyers, mostly from Malaysia, Singapore and Hong Kong, executives involved in negotiations said.
As well as potential regional buyers, foreign houses such as Banque Nationale de Paris, Merrill Lynch, Banque Paribas, Vickers Ballas and Credit Lyonnais are linked to some of the suspended firms.
At least one firm offer had been made for a smaller suspended firm, and foreign buyers had made a number of bids for the more attractive securities operations, executives said.
But the Bank of Thailand had resisted calls from potential buyers to take holdings only in the securities operations of the firms, an investment banker said.
Five large finance and securities firms, selected by the central bank to head any compulsory mergers from among the failed 16, are waiting to pick at the leftovers.
Krungthai Thanakit Plc, Dhana Siam Plc, Phatra Thanakit Plc, Nava Finance and Securities Plc and National Finance and Securities Plc will head consolidating groups and may receive banking licences.

"The big uncertainty is the size of the net liabilities we must consume. Ideally we want to cherry-pick a firm's assets and persuade the central bank to take the liabilities," an executive at one of the five firms said.
Failure to do that might mean the firms would have to raise capital at a time when the Thai market is at near eight-year lows, or have to find their own foreign equity holders.
The five merger leaders wanted to take the largest of the 16 firms into their groups to ease the asssessment and absorption process, analysts said.
The three largest of the closed firms -- General Finance and Securities Plc, CMIC Finance and Securities Plc and Finance One Plc -- were the prime picks, executives said.
Nava seemed likely to absorb CMIC before proceeding with existing merger plans, executives said.
Government officials have indicated that Krungthai Thanakit is likely to take debt-ridden Finance One Plc, but the state-backed broker may also have to take some smaller firms.
Phatra Thanakit may then receive General Finance and Securities Plc and its linked General Asia Bank, which is only weeks away from an initial public offering.
Phatra might also take G.C.N. Finance Plc, although it has been in talks with a foreign buyer, executives said.
National Finance and Securities is tipped to receive a bank licence formerly awarded to property firm MBK Properties Plc, while Dhana Siam Plc may pick the rest.
Whatever the outcome it promises to be a bloody shake-up of the 91-company industry which some believe may see only 15-30 firms survive into the next century.

"When you cut out the bad pieces of meat you are going to be left with with some blood on the floor, but they had to do something," said Nimit Wongjariakul, senior vice president at Thaimex Finance and Securities Plc, one of the firms involved in merger plans.
